trans-unit.source: En-GB of High Voltage Electrical Safety: Essential Practices and Procedures

Are you prepared to work safely with high voltage electricity? In this comprehensive course, you'll discover the essential knowledge and practical steps needed to recognize and mitigate electrical hazards, select the right protective equipment, and respond confidently to emergencies. Whether you're refreshing your expertise or building a foundation, this course will empower you to stay safe, protect your team, and ensure compliance with industry standards in high voltage environments.

High voltage electricity is a powerful force that enables modern life, but it also presents unique and severe dangers. In this lesson, you'll learn why recognizing high voltage hazards is essential for anyone working in or around electrical systems. By understanding these risks, you’ll be better prepared to protect yourself and others, forming the foundation for all safe work practices covered in this course.

g.g: Identify the main hazards associated with high voltage electricity and explain why they are dangerous.
Describe the types of injuries and damage that can result from high voltage incidents.
Recognize key terminology and definitions related to high voltage work.
Apply fundamental safety principles to reduce risk when working with or near high voltage systems.

source.g: Review each flashcard to familiarize yourself with essential terminology before moving forward.
High Voltage
A voltage exceeding 1,000 volts AC or 1,500 volts DC, as defined by industry standards and safety regulations.
Standard Electrical Work
Tasks involving lower voltages, typically below 1,000 volts AC, with less severe hazards than high voltage work.
Energised
Connected to a source of electrical supply; capable of delivering dangerous current.
De-energised
Not connected to any source of electrical supply, but not necessarily isolated from all hazards.
Arc Flash
A sudden release of energy between conductors, causing intense heat, light, and pressure that can result in severe injury.

trans-unit.source: Why High Voltage is Uniquely Hazardous

High voltage electricity poses significantly greater dangers compared to standard electrical systems. The hazards associated with high voltage are often not immediately apparent, as the risks can be invisible and silent. Even brief contact can result in severe injury or death. Recognizing the unique dangers of high voltage is essential for maintaining safety and preventing accidents.
The Main Hazards of High Voltage Electricity

source.g: Expand each section to learn about the primary hazards associated with high voltage systems. Each hazard includes a real-world example or consequence to help you recognize and remember the risks.

High voltage can cause rapid heating of skin and deep tissue, resulting in severe burns both on the surface and inside the body. Even brief exposure can lead to second-degree burns at energy levels as low as 1.2 calories per square centimeter per second.
For example, a worker accidentally contacting a live conductor may suffer deep tissue burns that require extensive medical treatment.

An arc flash is a sudden, explosive release of energy between conductive objects. This can create a powerful blast wave, intense heat, and airborne shrapnel, all of which pose serious risks to anyone nearby.
For instance, a tool dropped near energized equipment can trigger an arc flash, causing burns and injuries to multiple workers in the vicinity.
High voltage can trigger rapid, involuntary muscle contractions, making it impossible to release a live conductor once contact is made. This increases the duration and severity of the shock.
A real-world consequence is a worker becoming trapped, unable to let go, with electricity continuing to flow through their body.

High voltage incidents can ignite surrounding materials, cause explosions, and result in major damage to equipment and infrastructure. The thermal energy released can set clothing and nearby objects on fire.
For example, an electrical fault in a high voltage panel may lead to a fire that spreads rapidly throughout a facility.

High voltage can arc through air, creating a dangerous electrical bridge between the source and a person or object nearby. This means you can be injured without ever directly touching a live conductor.
A worker standing too close to energized equipment may be injured by an arc that jumps the gap, even without physical contact.

Thermal energy that can ignite clothing or nearby materials
Rapid, involuntary muscle contractions preventing release
Inability to let go of a live conductor due to body response

High voltage hazards are extremely dangerous but can be avoided. The key to prevention is recognizing potential dangers and being properly prepared. Awareness and readiness are your best protection against high voltage risks.
Now that you understand the hazards, let’s focus on the core safety principles that will guide your actions when working with or near high voltage systems.

source.g: Understanding and applying key electrical safety principles is essential for anyone working with high voltage systems. The following five principles are fundamental to ensuring your safety and the safety of those around you.
Assume All Circuits Are Live: Always treat every circuit as if it is energized until you have verified otherwise. This mindset prevents accidental contact with live parts.

Use the Right PPE: Wear insulated gloves, dielectric boots, face shields, and flame-resistant clothing designed for high voltage environments. The correct PPE can mean the difference between a close call and a serious injury.
Follow Lockout-Tagout Procedures: Ensure all equipment is de-energized, locked, and tagged before starting any work. This process protects you and your team from unexpected energization.

Maintain Safe Distances: High voltage can arc through air, so always keep the minimum safe approach distance based on voltage levels. Never assume you are safe just because you are not touching the equipment.

trans-unit.source: True or False: You should always assume all circuits are live until proven otherwise.
Correct. Assuming all circuits are live is the most important safety principle in high voltage work.
Incorrect. Never assume a circuit is safe until you have verified it is de-energized.

source.g: In this lesson, you explored the unique hazards of high voltage electricity, including severe burns, arc flashes, involuntary muscle contractions, and the potential for fires and explosions. You learned why high voltage is especially dangerous and how indirect contact can still result in injury. By mastering the key safety principles—such as always assuming circuits are live, using the right PPE, and following lockout-tagout procedures—you are taking essential steps to protect yourself and your team.
Remember, hazard recognition and preparation are your strongest defenses against electrical incidents. Carry these lessons forward as you continue your training.

trans-unit.source: Before any high voltage work begins, thorough preparation and strict adherence to procedures are non-negotiable. This lesson will show you why careful planning and compliance with safety protocols are essential—not just for regulatory reasons, but because lives depend on it. Building on your understanding of high voltage hazards, you'll now learn the practical steps that keep you and your team safe before the work even starts.

source.g: This lesson will equip you with the necessary knowledge and skills to safely prepare for and conduct high voltage work. You will learn about critical preparation steps, safety analysis, and essential procedures to maintain a safe work environment.
Identify Key Preparation Steps: Recognize the essential actions required before starting high voltage work.
Conduct Job Safety Analysis: Understand how to perform and participate in a job safety analysis and pre-work inspection.

The Three Pillars of Workplace Preparation

source.g: Explore the foundational elements that must be in place before any high voltage work begins. Expand each section to understand what is required and why it matters.

Only those who are properly trained, authorized, and competent should perform high voltage work. This includes having up-to-date site inductions and being able to demonstrate knowledge of electrical safety rules, rescue, and resuscitation procedures.
If you are not authorized, you must always be accompanied and supervised by someone who is.

Before starting any job, a thorough job safety analysis must be completed with your entire work party. All tools and personal protective equipment (PPE) should be inspected to ensure they are fit for use.
Testing devices must be calibrated and functioning, and warning signs and barriers need to be in place and clearly visible.
High voltage work is never a solo task. Only authorized personnel should participate, and anyone not fully authorized must be supervised at all times.
Team communication and readiness are critical to ensure everyone understands their role and the safety procedures in place.
Review each flashcard to reinforce the key elements of a thorough pre-work inspection. These steps help ensure the work environment is safe before any high voltage tasks begin.
Job Safety Analysis
A structured review of the work to identify hazards and plan controls before starting any high voltage task.
Tool and PPE Inspection
Carefully check all tools and personal protective equipment for damage or defects to confirm they are safe and suitable for use.
Calibration and Signage
Confirm that all testing devices are properly calibrated and that warning signs and barriers are in place and clearly visible.
Preparation saves lives. Rushing or skipping any step can lead to catastrophic consequences.

trans-unit.source: DNOT Procedures: Your Last Line of Defense

source.g: Do Not Operate Tag (DNOT) procedures are your critical safeguard against accidental energization. Strictly following each step in the correct order is essential—there is no room for shortcuts when safety is on the line.

trans-unit.source: The DNOT procedure is a sequence of actions designed to ensure that electrical equipment cannot be accidentally energized while work is underway. Each step must be completed in order for maximum safety.

source.g: The DNOT procedure is a sequence of actions designed to ensure that electrical equipment cannot be accidentally energized while work is underway. Each step must be completed in order for maximum safety.
Turn off and isolate all sources of electrical energy before beginning any work. Verify that all switches and disconnects are in the off position and that no power is present.
Attach locks and Do Not Operate tags to all switches and disconnects. This prevents anyone from accidentally re-energizing the equipment while work is in progress.
Use approved testing devices to confirm that no voltage is present. Always test after de-energizing and locking/tagging, never before. This step verifies that the equipment is truly safe to touch.
Only after all previous steps are completed and confirmed should work begin. Skipping or reordering steps can result in serious injury or death.
Following the DNOT procedure—De-energize, Lock/Tag, Test, Begin Work—ensures a safe environment for everyone involved. Never assume a step can be skipped or done out of order.

trans-unit.source: Test your understanding of the DNOT procedure by arranging the steps in the correct order. Getting this sequence right is critical for safety.
You’re preparing to work on a high voltage switch. The area is clear. What is the first step in the DNOT process?
Not yet. You must de-energize all electrical sources before applying locks and tags.
Correct! The first step is to de-energize before applying any locks or tags.
Not quite. Testing for absence of voltage comes after de-energizing the equipment.
Not safe. You must de-energize and verify absence of voltage before beginning work.
What Can Go Wrong? — Consequences of Skipping DNOT Steps

source.g: Explore the risks associated with skipping any step in the DNOT procedure. Each section highlights a potential consequence and why strict compliance is essential.
If you fail to de-energize equipment, live voltage may still be present, putting anyone who touches it at immediate risk of severe shock or electrocution.
Even a momentary lapse can result in life-threatening injuries.
Without locks and tags, someone else could unknowingly re-energize the equipment while you are working on it.
This can cause sudden, unexpected energization and catastrophic injury.
Assuming equipment is safe without testing can lead to a “false safe” situation, where hidden voltage remains present.
This step is your final confirmation that it is truly safe to begin work.
Strict compliance with DNOT procedures is mandatory—no shortcuts, no exceptions.

In this lesson, you learned about the three pillars of workplace preparation: training and competency, thorough pre-work inspections, and team readiness. You also mastered the DNOT procedure—De-energize, Lock/Tag, Test, and Begin Work—and saw how skipping any step can have severe consequences.

trans-unit.source: Hierarchy of Controls and PPE Selection
Hierarchy of Controls and PPE Selection

source.g: Welcome to this lesson on the hierarchy of controls and PPE selection in high voltage electrical safety. In this lesson, you'll learn how electrical risks are managed using a structured approach, and why personal protective equipment (PPE) is considered the last line of defense. Understanding and applying these concepts is essential for keeping yourself and your team safe when working with high voltage systems.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain the hierarchy of controls for electrical safety
Describe the role and limitations of PPE
Apply the five-step process for selecting PPE
Identify the minimum PPE requirements for high voltage work
Match PPE items to the hazards they protect against

trans-unit.source: Complete the content above before moving on.
The Hierarchy of Controls in Electrical Safety

source.g: Explore each level of the hierarchy of controls to understand how risks are managed in high voltage environments. Each control method plays a specific role in reducing danger, with PPE always being the last resort.
Elimination means completely removing the electrical hazard from the workplace. For example, decommissioning and removing unused high voltage equipment ensures it can no longer pose a risk.
This is the most effective control, but not always possible in operational environments.

Substitution involves replacing a hazardous process or equipment with something less dangerous. For instance, using lower voltage equipment where possible reduces the risk of severe electrical injury.
This control is effective but may not always be feasible for essential high voltage systems.
Isolation physically separates people from the hazard. Installing barriers, locked switchrooms, or remote switching devices ensures workers are not exposed to live high voltage parts.
Isolation reduces the chance of accidental contact and is a key control in electrical safety.

Engineering controls are design features that minimize risk, such as interlocks, insulation, and automatic shutdown systems. These controls help prevent incidents by making hazardous conditions less likely or less severe.
Engineering controls are built into equipment and systems to provide ongoing protection.
Administrative controls include procedures, training, signage, and supervision. Examples are safe work method statements, permits, and regular safety briefings.
These controls rely on people following rules and are most effective when combined with other controls.

PPE is the final barrier between the worker and the hazard. It includes items like gloves, helmets, and arc-rated clothing. PPE does not eliminate the hazard but provides protection if all other controls fail.
Always use PPE in conjunction with higher-level controls, never as the sole protection.

trans-unit.source: PPE is your last line of defense—never rely on it as your only protection.
The Five-Step Process for PPE Selection

source.g: To ensure you are properly protected, follow a structured five-step process for selecting PPE in high voltage and arc hazard environments. This process helps you make informed, standards-based decisions every time.

trans-unit.source: Choosing the right PPE is not guesswork—it requires a systematic approach. Follow these five steps to ensure your protection matches the hazards present.

source.g: Choosing the right PPE is not guesswork—it requires a systematic approach. Follow these five steps to ensure your protection matches the hazards present.
Identify all electrical and arc hazards in your work area. This includes recognizing sources of high voltage, potential for arc flash, and other risks.
For example, working near energized switchgear presents both shock and arc flash hazards.

trans-unit.source: Identify Assets with Arc Hazard Potential

source.g: Determine which equipment or locations could produce an arc flash. Focus on items like switchgear, transformers, and circuit breakers.
Not all equipment poses the same risk—prioritize areas with the highest arc hazard potential.
Calculate the incident energy or arc flash level for each identified asset. This is usually measured in calories per square centimeter and should be done by qualified personnel.
Knowing the exact energy level guides you in selecting PPE with the correct arc rating.

Use your organization’s risk management framework to evaluate the likelihood and consequences of an arc flash or electrical incident. Consider factors like work duration, proximity, and environmental conditions.
This assessment helps determine the level of protection and additional controls needed.
Based on the calculated hazard and risk assessment, choose PPE that meets or exceeds the required arc rating and complies with relevant standards.
Always consult with qualified personnel and never select PPE based on assumptions.
Following these five steps ensures your PPE selection is evidence-based, compliant, and tailored to the specific hazards of your work environment.

trans-unit.source: Which step in the PPE selection process involves calculating the incident energy exposure level?
This step is about recognizing hazards, not measuring them.
Identify Assets with Arc Hazard Potential
This step is about identifying where arc hazards may exist.
Correct! Quantifying the hazard means calculating the incident energy, which is critical for choosing the right PPE.
This step comes after you have calculated the hazard.

Minimum PPE Requirements for High Voltage Work

source.g: Review each flashcard to learn about the essential PPE items required for high voltage electrical work. Understanding what each item protects against is key to staying safe on the job.
Wrist to Ankle Clothing

trans-unit.source: Arc-rated shirts and trousers or overalls that cover all exposed skin, reducing the risk of burns and arc flash injury.

source.g: Enclosed Footwear with Hard Toe

trans-unit.source: Boots or shoes with a hard toe and full enclosure to protect feet from electrical hazards and falling objects.

source.g: Safety Glasses

trans-unit.source: Eye protection that shields against arc flash, flying debris, and projectiles during electrical work.

source.g: Safety Helmet

trans-unit.source: Head protection that guards against falling objects, bumps, and may provide electrical insulation.

source.g: Protective Gloves

trans-unit.source: Insulated gloves designed to protect hands from electrical shock, burns, and cuts.

source.g: Test your knowledge by matching each PPE item to the part of the body it protects. Drag each item to its correct category to reinforce your understanding of PPE functions.
Expand each section to see which PPE is required for different types of electrical hazards. Knowing the right protection for each risk is essential for effective safety management.
Arc-rated clothing and face shields are required to protect against the intense heat and energy of an arc flash. These items must meet recognized arc protection standards.
Always check the arc rating of your clothing and ensure face shields are rated for electrical work.
Insulated gloves and dielectric boots are essential for preventing electrical shock. These PPE items are tested to withstand high voltage exposure.
Use only gloves and boots that are certified for electrical protection and inspect them regularly.
Flame-resistant base garments provide protection against burns from electrical faults or arc flashes. These garments limit the severity of burn injuries.
Ensure all base garments meet flame resistance standards for electrical work.
Hard hats and reinforced footwear protect against injuries from falling tools or equipment. These items are especially important in areas with overhead hazards.
Choose PPE that is rated for both impact and electrical protection when required.

trans-unit.source: Roles, Responsibilities, and Safe Approach Distances
Roles, Responsibilities, and Safe Approach Distances

source.g: Welcome to this lesson on the critical human and spatial controls that keep high voltage work safe. While equipment and PPE are essential, true safety depends on clear roles, strict authorization, and a disciplined approach to proximity hazards. In this lesson, you'll learn how defined responsibilities and safe approach distances work together to prevent accidents and ensure every team member knows their part in maintaining a safe work environment.

This lesson will equip you with essential knowledge and skills for working safely around electrical hazards. By mastering the following objectives, you will be better prepared to ensure safety and compliance in your work environment.
Identify the three main roles and their responsibilities.
Explain access permit and isolation requirements.
Apply safe approach distances based on voltage.
Recognize special considerations for mobile plant and equipment.
Understand the critical function of supervision and separation.

trans-unit.source: Complete the content above before moving on.
Key Personnel Roles for High Voltage Work

source.g: Explore the three essential roles that form the backbone of safe high voltage operations. Each role has specific qualifications, responsibilities, and limitations that must be understood and respected to maintain a safe worksite.

An Authorised Person is someone with technical knowledge or sufficient experience, assessed as competent, and officially approved to carry out certain functions under safety rules. They are responsible for issuing access permits, supervising work, and ensuring all safety procedures are followed. For example, an Authorised Person might oversee the isolation and earthing of equipment before maintenance begins.

An Instructed Person works under the direct supervision of an Authorised Person. They are trained to avoid electrical dangers but cannot work independently on high voltage systems. For instance, an Instructed Person may assist with tasks during a shutdown, but only while being closely supervised.

The Safety Observer is specifically assigned to monitor work near electrical apparatus, warn against unsafe approaches, and provide emergency assistance if needed. They must remain vigilant and cannot be assigned other duties while observing. For example, a Safety Observer might halt work if someone or equipment gets too close to an exclusion zone.
Review these flashcards to understand the critical permissions and procedures that must be in place before any high voltage work begins.
What is an Access Permit?
An official document confirming that all isolation, de-energization, and earthing procedures have been completed, granting permission for work to proceed.
Isolation — What and Why?
Physically disconnecting all electrical sources to prevent any possibility of energization during work, ensuring a safe environment.
Prove Dead and Earthing
Verifying the absence of voltage with approved testers and applying earths at the worksite to protect against accidental energization or induced voltage.

trans-unit.source: Which role is responsible for issuing access permits?
Instructed Persons must be supervised and cannot issue permits.
Safety Observers monitor work but do not issue permits.
Only Authorised Persons have the authority to issue access permits.
Site Visitors are not permitted to issue access permits.
Only properly authorized and supervised personnel may access high voltage equipment—this is a non-negotiable safety rule.
Safe Approach Distances: Keeping People and Hazards Apart

source.g: Safe Approach Distances (SAD) are a cornerstone of electrical safety. These regulated distances create exclusion zones around energized conductors, ensuring that no person or object comes close enough to risk an electric arc or accidental contact. Even when equipment appears safe, maintaining these distances is vital to prevent serious injury or fatality.

trans-unit.source: Understanding and Applying Safe Approach Distances

source.g: Expand each section to learn what safe approach distances are, how they are determined, and how to apply them in real-world scenarios.

Safe Approach Distances are minimum separation zones established around exposed conductors or energized equipment. These distances are based on legal and industry standards and are designed to prevent accidental contact or arcing. Adhering to these zones is critical, as high voltage can arc through air even without direct contact.

Safe approach distances increase with voltage. For example, up to 300V requires 300mm, 15kV requires 640mm, 138-145kV requires 1300mm, and 500-550kV requires 3350mm. For the highest voltages, such as 765-800kV, the distance can be up to 4670mm. Mobile plant often requires even greater separation, such as 5.5m for personnel and 10m for equipment at 765kV.

trans-unit.source: How to Apply SAD in the Field

source.g: In practice, safe approach distances are enforced by marking boundaries, using barriers, and constant supervision. Workers must measure and respect these zones at all times, and any encroachment should trigger immediate corrective action. Always confirm the correct distance for the specific voltage before starting work.

trans-unit.source: Matching Voltage Levels to Safe Approach Distances

Review the voltage levels and their corresponding minimum safe approach distances. Drag each voltage to the correct category based on whether the distance applies to personnel or mobile plant. Pay special attention to the requirements for mobile plant.
Special Considerations for Mobile Plant and Equipment

source.g: Review these flashcards to understand the unique risks and requirements for mobile plant working near high voltage conductors.
Why does mobile plant require greater distances from high voltage conductors?
Mobile plant can move or sway unexpectedly, increasing the risk of breaching exclusion zones. Greater distances account for this movement and help prevent accidental contact.
What are the bonding and earthing requirements for mobile plant near electrical apparatus?
Mobile plant must be bonded to an established earth during work near electrical apparatus to prevent dangerous voltages from building up.
What should be done if no established earth is available for mobile plant?
If no established earth is available, a temporary earth spike shall be driven into the ground to bond the mobile plant and ensure safety.

trans-unit.source: Mobile plant is working near high voltage conductors but no established earth is available. What must be done?
Incorrect. Mobile plant must always be earthed.
A temporary earth spike shall be driven into the ground
Correct. A temporary earth spike must be used if no established earth is available.
Wait until an established earth becomes available
Incorrect. Work should not proceed without proper earthing, but a temporary solution is permitted.
The Safety Observer provides the earth connection
Incorrect. The Safety Observer does not provide the earth connection.
The Role of the Safety Observer

source.g: Expand each section to understand when a Safety Observer is required, their duties, and the strict limits of their role.

trans-unit.source: When is a Safety Observer Required?

source.g: A Safety Observer must be posted whenever there is a risk that a person, equipment, or mobile plant might inadvertently infringe safe approach distances. This is determined by a risk assessment before work begins.

trans-unit.source: Duties and Authority of the Safety Observer

source.g: The Safety Observer is responsible for monitoring work, warning against approach distance infringements, and has the authority to temporarily suspend work if safety is compromised. They must also be capable of providing emergency assistance and first aid if needed.

The Safety Observer cannot be assigned any other tasks while observing. Their sole focus must be on maintaining vigilance and ensuring that no one breaches the exclusion zone. This strict limitation is essential for effective supervision and accident prevention.

trans-unit.source: Can a Safety Observer be assigned other tasks while responsible for observing safe approach distances?
Yes, if the tasks are minor
Incorrect. The observer cannot be distracted by any other tasks.
Yes, if approved by an Authorised Person
Incorrect. No exceptions are allowed for the observer's focus.
No, the observer must focus solely on observing
Correct. The observer's only duty is to maintain vigilance on safe approach distances.
Incorrect. The observer must remain focused at all times during work.
Maintaining safe approach distances and clearly defined roles is not just a best practice—it is a lifesaving measure.

source.g: In this lesson, you learned how clearly defined roles, strict authorization, and safe approach distances work together to protect everyone on a high voltage worksite. Only Authorised Persons can issue permits and supervise, Instructed Persons must always be supervised, and Safety Observers play a critical role in enforcing exclusion zones. You also explored how approach distances vary with voltage, the special requirements for mobile plant, and the non-negotiable focus required for supervision. In the next lesson, you’ll build on this foundation by learning about electromagnetic induction hazards and advanced control measures to further enhance your safety knowledge.

trans-unit.source: Electromagnetic Induction Hazards and Control Measures
Electromagnetic Induction Hazards and Control Measures

source.g: Working near high voltage lines involves more than just avoiding direct contact—some of the most dangerous hazards are invisible. Electromagnetic induction can create lethal voltages on equipment and conductors, even when they appear de-energized. In this lesson, you'll learn how to recognize, understand, and control these advanced hazards. Building on your knowledge of roles and safe approach distances, we now focus on field effects, exposure limits, and the critical procedures that keep you safe from induction risks.
This lesson will give you the knowledge to identify invisible risks and apply advanced controls to protect yourself and your team.
Explain electromagnetic induction hazards.
Distinguish electric and magnetic fields.
Recognize exposure limits and physiological effects.
Describe equipotential zone setup steps.
Verify induction hazard controls before work.

trans-unit.source: Complete the content above before moving on.

source.g: Expand each section to learn what electromagnetic induction is, why it is dangerous, and where these hazards are most likely to occur in high voltage environments.

Electromagnetic induction occurs when electric and magnetic fields from energized high voltage lines induce voltages onto nearby de-energized or non-commissioned conductors. For example, a de-energized line running parallel to an energized line can become dangerously charged, even if it is not directly connected to a power source.
This phenomenon is invisible but can create hazardous conditions for workers who may not expect voltage to be present on supposedly safe equipment.

Induced voltages can be high enough to cause severe electric shock or even death. These voltages may appear on lines or equipment that have been de-energized, creating a false sense of security. If a worker touches a conductor with induced voltage, current can flow through their body to ground, resulting in serious injury.
Because the hazard is not always obvious, strict controls and awareness are essential to prevent accidental contact with induced voltages.

Induction hazards are most common near energized and de-energized parallel lines, at stringing sites, and in environments where conductive objects run close to high voltage transmission lines. Examples include fences, pipelines, rail lines, or new lines being constructed beside live circuits.
Any situation where conductive materials are exposed to strong electric or magnetic fields from nearby energized lines can present a significant induction risk.
Review each flashcard to understand the differences between electric and magnetic fields, and the concept of equipotential fields—key to recognizing and controlling induction hazards.
Electric Fields

trans-unit.source: Produced by voltage on energized conductors. They can induce voltages on nearby objects, especially if insulated from ground.

source.g: Magnetic Fields

trans-unit.source: Created by current flowing through transmission lines. They induce voltages in parallel conductive objects, such as pipelines or de-energized lines.

source.g: Equipotential Field

trans-unit.source: Lines of equal voltage in the air around conductors. Understanding these helps prevent dangerous voltage differences at worksites.

source.g: Explore each section to learn about exposure limits for electric and magnetic fields, and the physiological effects these fields can have on the human body.

Occupational exposure to electric fields is limited to 10 kV/m, while the general public limit is 5 kV/m. Near energized conductors, electric field strengths can reach up to 16 kV/m at the surface of high voltage lines. These limits are set to protect against harmful effects and must be strictly observed.
Exceeding these limits increases the risk of electric shock and other health hazards for workers and the public.

For magnetic fields, the occupational exposure limit is 10,000 mG, and for the general public, it is 2,000 mG. Magnetic field strength depends on the current and distance from the conductor. For example, at 100 mm from a conductor carrying 500A, the field can reach 10,000 mG.
Occupational limits are higher because workers are generally healthier and better able to withstand exposure than the general public.

Exposure to strong electric and magnetic fields can cause nerve and muscle stimulation, unpleasant skin discharges, and visual phenomena called phosphenes (flashing lights in the eyes). While some effects are mild, exceeding exposure limits can lead to serious health risks and must be avoided.
Understanding these effects helps workers recognize symptoms of overexposure and reinforces the need for strict controls.

trans-unit.source: What is the occupational exposure limit for electric fields near high voltage conductors?
Incorrect. 5 kV/m is the limit for the general public, not occupational exposure.
Correct. 10 kV/m is the occupational exposure limit for electric fields near high voltage conductors.
Incorrect. 15 kV/m exceeds the safe occupational exposure limit.
Incorrect. 20 kV/m is well above the recommended limit and is unsafe.
Complete the content above before moving on.
Follow these six steps to establish a safe equipotential zone at worksites where induction hazards are present. Each step is essential—skipping any step can compromise safety.

source.g: Establishing an equipotential zone is crucial for protecting workers from electrical induction hazards. This process involves creating a safe area where all surfaces are at the same electrical potential, minimizing the risk of dangerous voltage differences. Carefully follow each step to ensure maximum safety at the worksite.
Lay earth mats around the perimeter of all machinery and equipment. Ensure there are no gaps where a worker could step off the mat onto bare ground. This provides a continuous safe surface.
Connect all mats to each other, earth stakes, and machinery using proper earthing lugs and bonding leads. This ensures all surfaces are at the same potential, reducing step and touch voltages.
Set up fencing around the inner edge of the matting to prevent accidental step-off. This physical barrier keeps workers within the protected zone.
Place a secondary fence outside the inner fence. The size and shape should be adapted to the specific site and equipment layout for added protection.

trans-unit.source: Bond All Conductive Items Inside Fencing

source.g: Ensure all conductive objects within the fenced area are bonded to the earth mats. This prevents hazardous voltage differences from developing on tools or equipment.

trans-unit.source: Create Entry/Exit Point with Insulated Walkway

source.g: Install insulated rubber matting between the inner and outer fences at a designated entry/exit point. This allows safe access for personnel entering or leaving the zone.
Before starting work, double-check that all steps have been completed correctly. A properly configured equipotential zone is critical for protecting workers from induction hazards.

Earthing at a stringing site completely eliminates all induced voltages

Verifying Equipotential Zone Integrity
Check that all mats are bonded, fences are installed, and there are no gaps or exposed ground in the protected area.
Earthing Conductors During Breaks

Notification alone does not prevent hazardous voltages.
Speed does not eliminate the risk of induced voltages.

Electrical emergencies can happen even in the safest workplaces. Knowing how to respond quickly and correctly is just as important as preventing incidents in the first place. This lesson will equip you with the knowledge and step-by-step actions needed to handle electrical incidents, protect yourself and others, and ensure compliance with workplace safety requirements.
After learning about hazard prevention and control, it's time to focus on what to do when things go wrong. Being prepared for emergencies can save lives and minimize harm—your response matters.

This lesson is designed to equip you with the essential knowledge and skills needed to respond effectively and safely during electrical emergencies and rescue operations. By mastering these objectives, you will be prepared to take decisive action in high-stress situations, ensuring both your safety and the safety of others.
Identify prerequisites for safe rescue operations.
Apply step-by-step victim rescue procedures.
Respond appropriately to mobile plant electrical contact incidents.
Understand and execute incident reporting and site preservation.
Recall critical actions in electrical emergencies.

source.g: Before attempting any rescue in an electrical emergency, certain safety conditions must be met. Expand each section to understand the critical prerequisites that protect both the rescuer and the victim.

All conductors must be isolated, proved de-energised, and earthed at every source by an Authorised Person before anyone attempts a rescue within safe approach distances. Skipping this step puts rescuers at extreme risk of becoming victims themselves.
Never assume a conductor is safe—always follow the full isolation and earthing procedure.

After verifying that the area is de-energised, working earths must be applied at the location. This ensures that any unexpected re-energisation or residual voltage is safely diverted, further protecting everyone involved.
Failing to apply working earths can result in dangerous surprises during rescue operations.

Once the immediate emergency is under control, standard safety procedures must be restored as soon as possible. This includes proper documentation, incident investigation, and returning to established safety protocols.
Neglecting to re-establish normal precautions can lead to further incidents or complicate investigations.

trans-unit.source: Review each flashcard to learn the essential actions for rescuing someone affected by electrical contact. Each step is critical for protecting both the victim and the rescuer.
Do Not Touch the Victim Directly
Never touch a victim who is in contact with a live conductor. Use a non-conductive object to separate them from the electrical source.
Immediately call for professional help. Provide clear information about the location and nature of the incident.
Only begin CPR or treat burns after the electrical danger has been eliminated. Never attempt first aid while the victim is still in contact with electricity.
Take only actions needed to prevent further harm. Leave the scene undisturbed for investigation once everyone is safe.
Report every incident, even minor ones, to your supervisor as soon as possible. Proper reporting helps prevent future accidents.
What must be completed before attempting a rescue inside safe approach distances?
Conductors must be isolated, proved de-energised, and earthed
Emergency services must arrive on site
A rescue plan must be documented
Correct! Conductors must be isolated, proved de-energised, and earthed at all sources of supply by an Authorised Person before rescue attempts.
Not quite right. Review the rescue prerequisites to ensure you understand the critical steps before attempting a rescue.
Your safety comes first—never attempt a rescue until all sources of electrical danger are controlled.
Emergency Response for Mobile Plant Contact

source.g: When mobile plant or vehicles accidentally contact live electrical equipment, the risks and required actions are different from standard rescue situations. Understanding and following the correct protocol is essential to prevent further injury or fatalities.
Review the steps below to learn how to respond safely and effectively in these high-risk scenarios.

trans-unit.source: Mobile Plant Contact Protocol — Four Steps
This protocol outlines the essential steps to follow if mobile plant equipment comes into contact with live electrical equipment, ensuring the safety of both operators and bystanders.

source.g: When mobile plant contacts live electrical equipment, unique hazards arise. The vehicle and surrounding ground may both be energized, creating life-threatening risks for anyone nearby.

trans-unit.source: Stay on the Vehicle if Safe

source.g: If you are on the vehicle, remain there unless it is unsafe to do so. The vehicle may be energized, and stepping off could complete a circuit to ground, resulting in severe injury or death.
Alert everyone nearby to stay clear of the vehicle and surrounding area. The ground around the vehicle may be energized, creating step and touch potential hazards for anyone approaching.

trans-unit.source: Do Not Attempt Rescue Until Confirmed Isolated and Earthed

source.g: No one should attempt to rescue or approach the vehicle until the electrical lines and equipment have been isolated and earthed by qualified personnel. Attempting rescue before this is confirmed puts everyone at risk.

If you must leave the vehicle due to immediate danger (such as fire), jump well clear without touching the vehicle and ground at the same time. Land with your feet together and shuffle away without lifting your feet to avoid step potential.
Following these steps ensures the safety of both the operator and bystanders. Never rush or improvise—stick to the protocol for the best chance of a safe outcome.

trans-unit.source: Mobile plant has accidentally contacted live electrical equipment. What should the operator do?
Stay on the vehicle if safe until confirmed the equipment is no longer energised
Call for help while touching the vehicle frame
Attempt to reverse away from the contact
That's right! The operator should stay on the vehicle if safe until the equipment is confirmed de-energised. Exiting could complete a circuit to ground.
Not quite right. The safest action in this situation is to remain on the vehicle until it is confirmed safe to exit.

source.g: After an electrical emergency, what you do next is just as important as your initial response. Explore each section to understand the critical steps for reporting and preserving the site.
All incidents, no matter how minor, must be reported to your immediate supervisor as soon as possible. Prompt reporting ensures that hazards are addressed and helps prevent future incidents.
Failing to report can allow dangerous conditions to go unnoticed and uncorrected.
Only take actions necessary to prevent further harm or damage. Leave the scene undisturbed so investigators can determine the cause and prevent recurrence.
Disturbing the site can destroy evidence and hinder the investigation process.
Incident investigations identify root causes and help improve safety procedures. Your accurate reporting and site preservation contribute to a safer workplace for everyone.
Neglecting these steps can result in missed lessons and repeated mistakes.

source.g: In electrical emergencies, every second counts—your knowledge and disciplined response protect both lives and livelihoods.

Remember, your actions in an emergency can make the difference between life and death, and between a safe workplace and repeated incidents.

High voltage electrical safety is built on a foundation of strict regulations and industry standards. These rules are not just guidelines—they are legal and professional requirements that protect lives and ensure safe workplaces. In this lesson, you’ll discover the key organizations and standards that govern high voltage safety, and you’ll have the opportunity to demonstrate your understanding through a comprehensive assessment. Mastery of these regulations is essential for every electrical worker, supervisor, and safety professional.

Key Organizations and Standards in High Voltage Electrical Safety

source.g: Expand each section to learn about the major organizations and standards that shape electrical safety practices worldwide. Understanding who sets the rules—and what those rules require—will help you work safely and confidently in any high voltage environment.

The IEC is a global organization that develops international standards for electrical, electronic, and related technologies. Their standards set the benchmark for high voltage equipment, installation, and safe work practices across many countries. For example, IEC standards define voltage thresholds and testing procedures used in high voltage operations.
Following IEC standards ensures that equipment and procedures meet internationally recognized safety levels, supporting both compliance and interoperability.

OSHA is the primary regulatory body for workplace safety in the United States. OSHA standards are legally enforceable and establish minimum safety requirements for employers and workers, including those related to electrical hazards. For example, OSHA mandates lockout/tagout procedures and safe approach distances for high voltage work.
Compliance with OSHA regulations is mandatory for all U.S. workplaces and is regularly audited to ensure ongoing safety.

NFPA 70E is a standard focused specifically on electrical safety in the workplace. It provides detailed guidance on safe work practices, selection of personal protective equipment (PPE), and arc flash hazard assessment. For instance, NFPA 70E outlines how to determine the correct PPE for various electrical tasks and how to assess arc flash boundaries.
Adhering to NFPA 70E helps organizations minimize the risk of electrical injuries and maintain a culture of safety.

trans-unit.source: Applying Standards and Regulations on the Job

source.g: Review each flashcard to understand how to put regulatory knowledge into action and maintain compliance every day.
Why is compliance with standards and regulations essential?
Legal, ethical, and practical reasons make following standards non-negotiable. Compliance protects lives, avoids penalties, and upholds professional reputation.
Where can you find current standards and regulations?
Access up-to-date standards through your organization’s safety resources, by consulting supervisors or safety personnel, and by regularly reviewing official updates.
Why is ongoing training and competency assessment important for compliance?
Regular assessment and refresher training are vital to ensure you remain compliant and up to date with the latest safety requirements.
